items.stem: A thermal insulator is a material that …
options: is a poor conductor of thermal energy
items.answer: is a poor conductor of thermal energy
items.markingKey: Insulators reduce the rate of thermal energy transfer.

items.stem: Engineers design a lunar lander. The mass is halved while the gravitational field strength stays the same. Explain how the weight changes.
items.answer: The weight halves.
items.markingKey: Using W = mg: weight ∝ mass; factor = 0.500 = 0.500. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A horse travels 135 m at a constant speed of 1.5 m/s. What is the time taken?
Suggest and explain two design features that make a wine glass stable.
items.answer: Wide base (feet spread out) and low centre of gravity (heavy base / weight kept low), so the line of action of the weight stays within the base when it is tilted.
items.markingKey: wide base with reason [1]; low CG with reason [1]; link to line of action of weight within base [1] [3]

items.stem: Nadia finds that an irregular piece of aluminium has a mass of 27 g. It is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 60 cm³ to 70 cm³. Calculate the density of the object.
items.answer: 2.7 g/cm³
items.markingKey: V = 70 − 60 = 10 cm³; ρ = 27/10 = 2.7 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Define one joule.
items.answer: The work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force.
items.markingKey: 1 N × 1 m [1]; in direction of force [1] [2]

items.stem: In which energy resource is electricity produced like this: up-and-down motion of waves drives a generator?
items.answer: waves
items.markingKey: Waves: up-and-down motion of waves drives a generator.

items.stem: Water at 100 °C is boiled away in a kettle. The mass is increased by 50%. State and explain how the energy needed to change state changes.
items.answer: The energy needed to change state increases by 50%.
items.markingKey: Using E = lm: energy needed to change state ∝ mass; factor = 1.50 = 1.50. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A type of glass has refractive index 1.513 for red light and 1.530 for violet light. White light enters the glass from air at an angle of incidence of 40°. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction for each colour. (b) Explain how this produces a spectrum.
items.answer: (a) red 25.1°, violet 24.8° (b) the colours travel in slightly different directions, so they separate; violet is bent more (smaller r).
items.markingKey: (a) sin r = sin i/n for each [2] (b) different angles → separation [1] [3]

items.stem: A forklift truck stands on a warehouse floor. The force is doubled while the contact area stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the pressure changes.
items.answer: The pressure doubles.
items.markingKey: Using p = F/A: pressure ∝ force; factor = 2.00 = 2.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A diagram of the sound wave from a vibrating guitar string (sound in air) shows 8 compressions spread over a distance of 1.4 m (from the first to the last compression). Calculate the wavelength.
items.markingKey: λ = 1.4/7 = 0.2 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Changing from a gas to a liquid is called …
items.answer: condensation
items.markingKey: Gas → liquid: condensing.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which equation gives kinetic energy? (b) A 2 kg book is lifted 1.5 m. What is its gain in GPE? (g = 9.8 N/kg)
items.answer: (a) Eₖ = ½mv² (b) 29.4 J
items.markingKey: (a) Kinetic energy = ½ × mass × speed². (b) mgΔh = 2 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 29.4 J.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how each feature of a vacuum flask reduces thermal energy transfer. (b) Explain how an increase in greenhouse gases leads to global warming.
items.answer: (a) Vacuum: no conduction or convection; silvered walls: reduce radiation (poor emitter/good reflector); stopper: reduces convection and evaporation; insulating supports: reduce conduction. (b) The Earth’s surface emits infrared; greenhouse gases absorb it and re-emit some back towards the Earth; more gases mean less energy escapes, so the Earth must warm until the outgoing rate again equals the incoming rate.
items.markingKey: (a) vacuum [1]; silvering [1]; stopper/supports [1] [3] (b) surface emits infrared [1]; gases absorb/re-emit [1]; imbalance → temperature rise [1] [3]

items.stem: A student whirls a bung of mass 200 g on a string in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m and measures the tension needed at different speeds: speed/m/s 2.0, 3.0, 4.0; tension/N 2.4, 5.4, 9.6. (a) Describe the trend. (b) Predict, with a reason, whether the tension needed at 3.0 m/s would be larger or smaller for a radius of 1.0 m.
items.answer: (a) The force needed increases as speed increases (more than proportionally). (b) Smaller: a larger radius needs a smaller force for the same speed and mass.
items.markingKey: (a) trend [1]; not proportional/increases faster [1] (b) smaller with reason [1] [3]

items.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 10 m/s in 6 s. Ethan calculates the distance travelled as 10 × 6 = 60 m. Explain the mistake and give the correct distance.
items.answer: Ethan used the area of a rectangle; the speed was not 10 m/s throughout. Area of triangle = ½ × 6 × 10 = 30 m.
items.markingKey: identifies rectangle instead of triangle / average speed is 5 m/s [1]; correct 30 m [1] [2]

items.stem: In a bottle opener, a force of 50 N acts at right angles to the opener at a perpendicular distance of 0.1 m from the pivot. Work out the moment of the force.
items.answer: 5 N m

items.answer: The power triples.

items.markingKey: input = 500/0.35 = 1430 MW. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain, in terms of particles, why the temperature of boiling water stays at 100 °C even though it is still being heated. (b) Explain why washing dries faster on a warm, windy day.
items.answer: (a) The energy supplied is used to overcome the attractive forces between particles so they escape as gas, not to increase their kinetic energy. (b) Warmer water molecules have more energy so more escape; wind removes the vapour so fewer molecules return to the liquid.
items.markingKey: (a) energy breaks forces/bonds [1]; KE (temperature) unchanged [1] [2] (b) temperature effect [1]; wind removes vapour [1] [2]

items.stem: A ray inside a block of glass (n = 1.5) meets the glass–air boundary at an angle of incidence of 45°. Calculate the critical angle and state what happens to the ray.
items.answer: c = 41.8°; total internal reflection.

items.stem: A point at the bottom of an oil storage tank is 4 m below the surface of oil (density 800 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg). Work out the pressure due to the liquid.
items.markingKey: Δp = ρgΔh = 800 × 9.8 × 4 = 31 400 Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Sound travels at about 4000 m/s in wood and 340 m/s in air. Explain this difference in terms of particles, and state in which material a sound would take less time to travel 1 km.
items.answer: Wood: particles are closer together / more strongly linked, so vibrations pass on faster; it takes 0.25 s compared with 2.94 s.
items.markingKey: particle explanation [1]; correct material [1]; times [1] [3]

items.stem: Air in a weather balloon (at roughly constant temperature) has a volume of 6 m³ at a pressure of 200 kPa. The volume changes to 15 m³ at constant temperature. Determine the new pressure.
items.answer: 80 kPa
items.markingKey: p₂ = p₁V₁/V₂ = 200 × 6/15 = 80 kPa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Draw (describe) an energy transfer diagram for the following: a stretched catapult fires a stone. Label the stores and the transfer pathway.
items.answer: Elastic (strain) store → (mechanically by the force of the elastic) → kinetic store, with a branch to the thermal store of the surroundings (wasted).
items.markingKey: correct starting store [1]; correct useful final store [1]; pathway/wasted branch [1] [3]

(a) State which surface is the best emitter. (b) Explain how the results show this. (c) State two variables that should be controlled.
items.answer: (a) dull (matt) black (b) it cooled the most (largest temperature drop in the same time). (c) same volume and starting temperature of water; same can size; same room conditions/no draughts; lids on.
items.markingKey: (a) correct surface [1] (b) largest drop in same time [1] (c) two controls [2] [4]

items.markingKey: W = 882 N; resultant = 882 − 529 = 353 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Freya and Ethan walk along the same path. On a distance-time graph, Freya’s line is straight with gradient 3 m/s and Ethan’s is straight with gradient 8 m/s. Compare their motion and state who reaches a point 120 m along the path first.
items.answer: Both move at constant speed; Ethan is faster. Times: Freya 40 s, Ethan 15 s, so Ethan arrives first.
items.markingKey: both constant speed [1]; compares gradients [1]; correct conclusion with times [1] [3]

items.stem: On a uniform metre rule balanced at its centre, load P of weight 3 N is 12 cm from the pivot on one side. Load Q of weight 0.5 N is on the other side. The system balances. Work out the distance of load Q from the pivot.
items.answer: 72 cm

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student uses a 30 cm ruler to measure the length of a corridor about 12 m long. Explain why this is a poor choice and suggest a better instrument. (b) Explain why the zero end of a worn ruler should not be used as the starting point for a measurement.
items.answer: (a) The ruler must be moved many times, so small errors add up at each move; a measuring tape or trundle wheel covers the length in one measurement. (b) The end may be damaged so 0 is not at the true zero (zero error); start from another mark such as 1.0 cm and subtract it.
items.markingKey: (a) errors accumulate with repeated moves [1]; tape measure / trundle wheel [1] [2] (b) zero error from worn end [1]; start from another mark and subtract [1] [2]

items.markingKey: useful energy = mgh = 118 000 J [1]; useful power = 11 800 W [1]; efficiency = 80% [1] [3]

items.stem: Almost all of our energy resources depend on the Sun. (a) Explain how energy travels from the Sun to the Earth. (b) Name two energy resources that do not depend on the Sun. (c) Explain how the Sun is the source of energy for wind power.
items.answer: (a) As electromagnetic radiation, which can travel through a vacuum. (b) Tidal, geothermal (and nuclear fission). (c) Uneven heating of the Earth causes convection currents in the atmosphere.
items.markingKey: (a) As electromagnetic radiation [1]; which can travel through a vacuum [1] [2] (b) Tidal [1]; geothermal (and nuclear fission) [1] [2] (c) Uneven heating of the Earth causes convection currents in the atmosphere (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2]

items.stem: A steel bridge 100 m long increases in length by 12 mm for every 10 °C rise. The temperature ranges from 0 °C in winter to 40 °C above that in summer. (a) Calculate the total change in length. (b) Explain why engineers include expansion gaps or joints.
items.answer: (a) 48 mm (b) without gaps the expanding structure would push against fixed points, causing large forces that could buckle or crack it.
items.markingKey: (a) 12 × 40/10 [1] = 48 mm [1] (b) prevents buckling / large forces [1]; particle explanation of expansion [1] [4]

State the new distance between person and image.
items.answer: (a) 4 m (b) Virtual, upright, same size (laterally inverted). (c) 35° (d) Rays do not actually meet there; they only appear to come from behind the mirror. (e) 3 m

items.stem: Two springs A (k = 25 N/m) and B (k = 20 N/m) are tested by Hana. (a) Calculate the extension of A for a load of 4 N. (b) Describe how the load-extension graphs of the two springs would differ. (c) Suggest which spring would be better for a newton meter that must measure forces up to 1 N precisely, and why.
items.answer: (a) 0.16 m (b) Both straight lines through the origin (in the linear region); the stiffer spring has the steeper line if load is on the y-axis. (c) B: lower k gives larger extension per newton, so readings are more precise.

items.stem: A fishing boat near Karachi uses sonar. (a) The echo returns after 0.6 s (speed in water 1500 m/s). Calculate the depth. (b) A shoal of fish passes under the boat. Describe what the operator sees on the display. (c) Explain why a pulse, rather than a continuous wave, is used. (d) Give one other use of ultrasound.
items.answer: (a) 450 m (b) An extra echo arriving earlier than the sea-bed echo. (c) So that the time for each reflection can be measured. (d) Prenatal scanning / crack detection / cleaning.

items.stem: Gas at 200 kPa acts on a square panel of a sealed tank of area 0.5 m². (a) Calculate the force on it. (b) The gas is heated at constant volume and the pressure rises by 20%. Calculate the new force. (c) Explain the increase using the kinetic particle model.
items.answer: (a) 100 000 N (b) 120 000 N (c) particles move faster, hitting the surface more often and harder.

items.stem: Daniel adds a few grains of potassium permanganate to one corner of a tank of water and heats beneath them. (a) Explain why the dye rises above the flame. (b) Explain why this cannot happen in a solid. (c) Predict what would happen if the beaker were heated at the top instead. (d) Name one everyday device that relies on this process.
items.answer: (a) The water there is heated, expands, becomes less dense and rises. (b) Particles in a solid cannot flow from place to place. (c) Hot water would stay at the top (less dense); little convection, so the bottom stays cool. (d) Kettle / hot-water tank / radiator / fridge.

items.stem: A saucepan has a copper base and a plastic handle. (a) Explain why the base of the pan is made of copper. (b) Describe how energy is conducted through the copper base. items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A 2 kg book is lifted 1.5 m. What is its gain in GPE? (g = 9.8 N/kg) (b) Which equation gives the change in gravitational potential energy?

(b) Different resources have different strengths: reliable ones (nuclear, gas, hydro) cover base load and peaks, while renewables cut emissions; a mix protects supply when one is unavailable.

items.stem: 33 400 J is needed to melt 0.1 kg of ice at constant temperature. Work out the specific latent heat.
items.markingKey: l = E/m = 33 400/0.1 = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: For a person standing on the floor, one force is: "the floor pushes up on the person". State the Newton’s third law partner of this force and give two ways in which the two forces are the same.
items.answer: The person pushes down on the floor. They are equal in size, of the same type, act along the same line (but in opposite directions on different objects).
items.markingKey: partner force [1]; any two of: equal size, same type, same line [2] [3]

items.stem: Two forces act on a boat being rowed against the wind along the same line in opposite directions: 300 N to the right and 80 N to the left. Work out the resultant force (to the right).
items.markingKey: R = 300 − 80 = 220 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The cooling fins on the back of a refrigerator are painted dull black. Explain why, using ideas about thermal radiation.
items.answer: Dull black surfaces are good emitters, so they radiate energy away quickly; fins give a large surface area.
items.markingKey: surface property (absorber/emitter/reflector) [1]; applied to context [1] [2]

items.stem: An engine pushes a train with a force of 125 kN through 100 m. Calculate the work done in J.
items.markingKey: convert to N and m [1]; W = Fd [1] = 1.25 × 10⁷ J [1] [3]

items.stem: The refractive index of diamond is 2.42. Calculate the critical angle.
items.markingKey: sin c = 1/2.42; c = sin⁻¹(1/2.42) = 24.4°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 25 m/s in 8 s. Diego calculates the distance travelled as 25 × 8 = 200 m. Explain the mistake and give the correct distance.
items.answer: Diego used the area of a rectangle; the speed was not 25 m/s throughout. Area of triangle = ½ × 8 × 25 = 100 m.
items.markingKey: identifies rectangle instead of triangle / average speed is 12.5 m/s [1]; correct 100 m [1] [2]

items.stem: Radiation from the Sun delivers 1100 J each second to every square metre of a surface facing it. Calculate the energy reaching an area of 1 m² in 600 s.
items.markingKey: 1100 × 1 × 600 = 6.60 × 10⁵ J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A diver investigates pressure underwater. The depth is halved while the density of the liquid stays the same. Explain how the pressure due to the liquid changes.
items.answer: The pressure due to the liquid halves.
items.markingKey: Using Δp = ρgΔh: pressure due to the liquid ∝ depth; factor = 0.500 = 0.500. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A solar panel is supplied with 2000 J. It transfers 1500 J usefully and 400 J to the internal store of its surroundings by heating; the rest is transferred as sound. Calculate the energy transferred as sound and state the principle you used.
items.answer: 100 J; conservation of energy (total output = input).
items.markingKey: principle of conservation [1]; 2000 − 1500 − 400 [1] = 100 J [1] [3]

items.stem: A microphone connected to an oscilloscope shows one full wave every 5 divisions at 5 ms per division. (a) Calculate the period. (b) Calculate the frequency. (c) State whether the sound is audible to humans, giving a reason. (d) Describe the trace for a quieter sound of the same pitch.
items.answer: (a) 0.025 s (b) 40 Hz (c) Yes (d) Same spacing, smaller height.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.025 s [1] (b) correct method/substitution [1]; answer 40 Hz with unit [1] [2] (c) Yes [1] (d) Same spacing [1]; smaller height [1] [2]

items.stem: A gas at 25 °C is heated until the average kinetic energy of its particles doubles. (a) Convert 25 °C to kelvin. (b) Calculate the final temperature in K and in °C. (c) Explain why you cannot simply double 25 °C.
items.answer: (a) 298 K (b) 596 K = 323 °C (c) average KE is proportional to the Kelvin temperature; the Celsius zero is not absolute zero.

items.stem: Yusuf heats crushed ice and records the temperature every 30 s until it has been boiling for a few minutes. (a) Explain why the temperature stays at 0 °C while the ice melts. (b) Describe what happens to the particles when the water then boils. (c) State two differences between this boiling and the evaporation of water from a puddle. (d) Explain why water left in a beaker cools as it evaporates.
items.answer: (a) Energy is used to break bonds between particles, not to raise their KE. (b) They gain enough energy to overcome attractive forces completely and escape as a gas throughout the liquid. (c) Boiling at 100 °C throughout the liquid with bubbles; evaporation at any temperature from the surface only. (d) The most energetic particles escape, so the average KE of the remaining particles falls.
items.markingKey: (a) Energy is used to break bonds between particles [1]; not to raise their KE [1] [2] (b) They gain enough energy to overcome attractive forces completely and escape [1]; as a gas throughout the liquid [1] [2] (c) Boiling at 100 °C throughout the liquid with bubbles [1]; evaporation at any temperature from the surface only [1] [2] (d) The most energetic particles escape [1]; so the average KE of the remaining particles falls [1] [2]

items.stem: A cannon of mass 1000 kg, mounted on a frictionless track, fires a cannonball of mass 8 kg forwards at 150 m/s. Both are initially at rest. (a) State the total momentum before firing. (b) Explain why the recoil speed is much smaller than the speed of the cannonball. (c) Compare the kinetic energies after firing and explain where the energy came from.
items.answer: (a) 0 (b) Equal momentum but much larger mass, so smaller speed. (c) cannonball: 90 000 J; launcher: 720 J; from chemical (or elastic) energy.
items.markingKey: (a) 0 [1] (b) Equal momentum but much larger mass [1]; so smaller speed [1] [2] (c) both KEs [2]; source [1] [3]

items.stem: A crystal of purple dye is placed at one side of the bottom of a beaker of water and the beaker is heated gently beneath the crystal. (a) Explain why the dye rises above the flame. (b) Explain why this cannot happen in a solid. (c) Predict what would happen if the beaker were heated at the top instead. (d) Name one everyday device that relies on this process.
items.answer: (a) The water there is heated, expands, becomes less dense and rises. (b) Particles in a solid cannot flow from place to place. (c) Hot water would stay at the top (less dense); little convection, so the bottom stays cool. (d) Kettle / hot-water tank / radiator / fridge.
items.markingKey: (a) The water there is heated [1]; expands, becomes less dense and rises [1] [2] (b) Particles in a solid cannot flow from place to place [1] (c) Hot water would stay at the top (less dense) [1]; little convection, so the bottom stays cool [1] [2] (d) Kettle / hot-water tank / radiator / fridge [1]

items.stem: Two plane mirrors are placed with an angle of 70° between their reflecting surfaces. A ray strikes the first mirror with an angle of incidence of 40° and then reflects onto the second mirror. (a) State the angle of reflection at the first mirror. (b) Calculate the angle of incidence at the second mirror. (c) State the law you used.
items.answer: (a) 40° (b) 30° (c) angle of incidence = angle of reflection (from the normal).
items.markingKey: (a) 40° [1] (b) ray makes 50° with mirror 1; triangle gives 60° with mirror 2 [1]; i₂ = 90 − 60 = 30° [1] (c) law of reflection [1] [4]

items.stem: Consider a ball dropped from a tall bridge in Nairobi. (a) Calculate the speed after 2.5 s, ignoring air resistance. (b) Calculate the distance fallen in 2.5 s. (c) Describe how the graph changes when air resistance is significant. (d) State the acceleration at the start of the fall and explain.
items.answer: (a) 24.5 m/s (b) 30.6 m (c) The gradient decreases as speed increases; the curve levels off at terminal velocity. (d) 9.8 m/s²: at the start speed is zero, so air resistance is zero and only weight acts.
items.markingKey: (a) v = gt = 9.8 × 2.5 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 24.5 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) area = ½ × 2.5 × 24.5 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 30.6 m with unit [1] [2] (c) decreasing gradient [1]; levels off [1] [2] (d) g [1]; no air resistance at v = 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: Consider a satellite in orbit, moving at a steady speed in a circle. (a) State the direction of the resultant force. (b) Explain why the object is accelerating even if its speed is constant. (c) Describe what would happen if this force suddenly stopped acting. (d) State how the force must change if the speed increases but the radius stays the same.
items.answer: (a) Towards the centre of the circle. (b) Velocity is a vector; its direction keeps changing. (c) It would move off in a straight line along the tangent at constant speed. (d) It must increase.
items.markingKey: (a) Towards the centre of the circle [1] (b) Velocity is a vector [1]; its direction keeps changing [1] [2] (c) straight line [1]; tangent [1] [2] (d) It must increase [1]

items.stem: A ray of light passes from air into ice (refractive index 1.31) with an angle of incidence of 20°. Calculate the angle of refraction.
A town near Dubai is considering solar-cell power. (a) Describe how electricity is generated using solar cells. (b) State whether the energy originally came from the Sun. (c) Give two disadvantages.
items.answer: (a) Light is transferred directly to electrical energy in photovoltaic cells. (b) Yes (c) no output at night, low in cloud; large area needed.
items.markingKey: (a) Light is transferred directly to electrical energy in photovoltaic cells (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) Yes [1] (c) no output at night, low in cloud [1]; large area needed [1] [2]

items.stem: A mass of 4.08 kg hung on a trampoline spring stretches it by 1 cm (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the weight of the mass. (b) Calculate the spring constant. (c) Calculate the extension for a load of 80 N, assuming the limit of proportionality is not reached.

A ball of mass 0.5 kg starts from rest at the top of a long slope 10 m high (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the GPE lost in reaching the bottom. (b) Calculate the speed at the bottom if no energy is wasted. (c) Explain why the actual speed does not depend on the mass if the same percentage is wasted.
items.answer: (a) 49 J (b) 14 m/s (c) Both GPE and KE are proportional to m, so m cancels.
items.markingKey: (a) mgΔh (method/substitution) [1]; answer 49 J with unit [1] [2] (b) mgh = ½mv² [1]; v = √(2gh) [1] [2] (c) Both GPE and KE are proportional to m [1]; so m cancels [1] [2]

items.stem: A fishing boat near Jakarta uses sonar. (a) State what is meant by ultrasound. (b) The echo returns after 1.0 s (speed in water 1500 m/s). Calculate the depth. (c) A shoal of fish passes under the boat. Describe what the operator sees on the display. (d) Explain why a pulse, rather than a continuous wave, is used. (e) Give one other use of ultrasound.
items.answer: (a) Sound with frequency above 20 kHz. (b) 750 m (c) An extra echo arriving earlier than the sea-bed echo. (d) So that the time for each reflection can be measured. (e) Prenatal scanning / crack detection / cleaning.
items.markingKey: (a) Sound with frequency above 20 kHz [1] (b) vt/2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 750 m with unit [1] [2] (c) An extra echo arriving earlier than the sea-bed echo (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (d) So that the time for each reflection can be measured [1] (e) Prenatal scanning / crack detection / cleaning [1]

items.stem: Lead melts at 327 °C and boils at 1749 °C. (a) State the state of lead at 317 °C. (b) State the state of lead at 1759 °C. (c) Explain what happens to the particles when the substance melts.
items.answer: (a) Solid. (b) Gas. (c) They gain energy and vibrate more until they break free of fixed positions and can move past each other.
items.markingKey: (a) Solid [1] (b) Gas [1] (c) They gain energy and vibrate more until they break free of fixed positions and can move past each other (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2]

items.stem: A filing cabinet has a base 1.6 m wide and its centre of gravity is 2 m above the centre of the base. Calculate the angle through which it can be tilted about one edge before it topples.
items.markingKey: topples when CG is vertically above the edge [1]; tan θ = 0.8/2 [1]; θ = 21.8° [1] [3]

items.stem: A concrete motorway section 100 m long increases in length by 12 mm for every 10 °C rise. The temperature ranges from 5 °C in winter to 40 °C above that in summer. (a) Calculate the total change in length. (b) Explain why engineers include expansion gaps or joints.
items.answer: (a) 48 mm (b) without gaps the expanding structure would push against fixed points, causing large forces that could buckle or crack it.
items.markingKey: (a) 12 × 40/10 [1] = 48 mm [1] (b) prevents buckling / large forces [1] [3]

items.stem: A wingsuit flyer of mass 70 kg jumps from a cliff. (g = 9.8 N/kg) (a) Calculate the weight. (b) Explain why the acceleration decreases as the speed increases. (c) Sketch-describe the speed-time graph from jumping until just before the parachute opens.
items.answer: (a) 686 N (b) Air resistance increases, so resultant force (W − drag) decreases; a = F/m. (c) Curve starting at origin with gradient 9.8 m/s², becoming less steep, levelling off at terminal velocity.
items.markingKey: (a) W = mg: 686 N [1] (b) Air resistance increases [1]; so resultant force (W − drag) decreases, a = F/m [1] [2] (c) curve from origin [1]; levels off [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya wants the thickness of one CD. The bottom of a stack of 20 identical CDs in a spindle is at the 1.5 cm mark of a ruler and the top is at 3.9 cm. (a) Calculate the thickness of one CD in mm. (b) Calculate the height of a stack of 40 of them in cm. (c) Explain why measuring a stack is better than measuring one CD.
items.answer: (a) 1.2 mm (b) 4.8 cm (c) one CD is too thin to measure precisely with a ruler; the reading error is shared over 20 items.
items.markingKey: (a) 3.9 − 1.5 = 2.4 cm; ÷ 20 = 1.2 mm [2] (b) 40 × 1.2 mm = 4.8 cm [1] (c) ruler resolution 1 mm too coarse for one item; error divided by number in stack [2] [5]

items.stem: A Leslie cube has four faces: matt black, shiny black, matt white and shiny silver. It is filled with boiling water. (a) Predict which face gives the highest reading on the infrared detector. (b) Predict which face gives the lowest reading. (c) Explain why the detector must be the same distance from each face. (d) Explain why the readings fall slowly during the experiment.
items.answer: (a) The matt (dull) black face. (b) The shiny silver face. (c) Intensity decreases with distance; for a fair test only the surface should change. (d) The water cools, and a cooler surface emits less radiation.
items.markingKey: (a) The matt (dull) black face [1] (b) The shiny silver face [1] (c) Intensity decreases with distance [1]; for a fair test only the surface should change [1] [2] (d) The water cools [1]; and a cooler surface emits less radiation [1] [2]

items.stem: An electric kettle rated at 2000 W heats 1.0 kg of water for 60 s. (a) Calculate the electrical energy transferred. (b) Only 108000 J reaches the water. Calculate the energy wasted. (c) Calculate the useful power. (d) Explain what is meant by a power of 2000 W. (e) Suggest why a more powerful kettle boils the same water faster.
items.answer: (a) 120000 J (b) 12000 J (c) 1800 W (d) 2000 J of energy is transferred each second. (e) It transfers the same energy at a greater rate, so less time is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) E = Pt (method/substitution) [1]; answer 120000 J with unit [1] [2] (b) 12000 J [1] (c) 1800 W [1] (d) 2000 J of energy is transferred each second [1] (e) It transfers the same energy at a greater rate [1]; so less time is needed [1] [2]
